content.title: Parallel Lines, Transversals, and Angle Relationships
content.overview: This lesson focuses on the various angle relationships formed when a line (transversal) intersects two parallel lines. Mastering these geometric properties is fundamental to solving complex geometry problems on the SAT.
learning_objectives: Identify and define vertical angles, supplementary angles, corresponding angles, alternate interior angles, and same-side interior angles.
Apply parallel line properties to calculate unknown angles.
Use angle relationships to determine if two lines are parallel.

sections.title: Basic Angle Relationships
sections.content:
Before studying parallel lines, you must master the basic relationships when two lines intersect:
1. **Vertical Angles**: Opposite angles formed by two intersecting lines. Vertical angles are always equal.
2. **Supplementary Angles**: Two adjacent angles on the same straight line. Their measures sum to 180°.

sections.title: Parallel Lines and Transversals
sections.content:
When a line (called a transversal) crosses two parallel lines, eight angles are formed. If line L1 is parallel to L2, the following properties hold:
1. **Corresponding Angles**: Angles in the same relative position are equal (e.g., top-left equals top-left).
2. **Alternate Interior Angles**: Angles located between the two parallel lines and on opposite sides of the transversal are equal.
3. **Alternate Exterior Angles**: Angles located outside the two parallel lines and on opposite sides of the transversal are equal.
4. **Consecutive/Same-side Interior Angles**: Angles located between the two parallel lines and on the same side of the transversal are supplementary (sum to 180°).

![Parallel Line Angle Relationships](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/619b15ac-45c4-4be2-b47a-7bafdc8dc18a-1786502171856-839.webp)

sections.title: Determining Parallel Lines
sections.content: The converse of the above properties is also true. If it is known that corresponding angles are equal, alternate interior angles are equal, or same-side interior angles are supplementary, then it can be concluded that the two lines are parallel.

worked_examples.question: Given that line L1 is parallel to L2. Transversal T intersects L1 to form a 70° angle. Find the measure of the angle that has a 'same-side interior' relationship with this angle.
worked_examples.solution:
Step 1: Identify the relationship. According to parallel line properties, same-side interior angles are supplementary.
Step 2: Set up the equation. Let the unknown angle be x, then 70° + x = 180°.
Step 3: Solve. x = 180° - 70° = 110°.
Conclusion: The measure of the angle is 110°.

common_mistakes: Incorrectly assuming angles are equal just because they are alternate interior angles, while ignoring the requirement that the lines must be parallel.
Confusing corresponding angles (which are equal) with same-side interior angles (which are supplementary).
Failing to correctly identify which two lines are parallel and which line is the transversal in complex geometric figures.
exam_tips: In SAT problems, if you see the word 'parallel' or the '||' symbol, immediately look for equal angles (corresponding, alternate interior).
If the figure looks parallel but the problem does not explicitly state it, never assume they are parallel.
Use the 'Z' shape to find alternate interior angles and the 'F' shape to find corresponding angles.
content.recap: When a transversal intersects parallel lines, all acute angles are equal, all obtuse angles are equal, and the sum of any one acute angle and any one obtuse angle is 180° (unless all angles are 90°).

knowledge_claims.content: Vertical angles are two non-adjacent angles with a common vertex formed by intersecting lines, and their measures are always equal.
Supplementary angles are two adjacent angles on a straight line whose measures sum to 180°.
When two parallel lines are intersected by a third line (transversal), the resulting corresponding angles are equal.
When two parallel lines are intersected by a transversal, alternate interior angles (located inside the parallel lines and on opposite sides of the transversal) are equal.
When two parallel lines are intersected by a transversal, the sum of the measures of same-side interior angles (located inside the parallel lines and on the same side of the transversal) equals 180°.
Alternate exterior angles are located outside the two parallel lines and on opposite sides of the transversal; they are equal when the lines are parallel.
If two lines are intersected by a third line and the corresponding angles are equal, then the two lines are parallel.
Parallelism cannot be judged by sight alone; it must be supported by text in the problem or geometric symbols like parallel arrows.
In a parallel line transversal model, if one angle is x, the angle not equal to it is typically 180 - x.
Alternate interior angles typically appear in a 'Z' or reverse 'Z' shape structure within a figure.
